reference.source: Standard cardiology and inherited cardiac conditions references
clinicalPearls: Caused by variants in PRKAG2, encoding the gamma-2 regulatory subunit of AMP-activated protein kinase, leading to cardiac glycogen accumulation
The characteristic triad is ventricular pre-excitation (Wolff-Parkinson-White pattern), left ventricular hypertrophy, and progressive conduction system disease
It mimics hypertrophic cardiomyopathy on imaging but is a glycogen storage disorder rather than a sarcomeric disease
Ventricular pre-excitation predisposes to supraventricular tachyarrhythmia, while conduction disease often progresses to atrioventricular block requiring pacing
Atrial fibrillation is common and may be poorly tolerated in the presence of an accessory pathway
Inheritance is autosomal dominant, so family screening with ECG and imaging is important
The combination of a short PR interval or delta wave with unexplained hypertrophy should raise suspicion of this diagnosis
reference.pathophysiology: PRKAG2 encodes a regulatory subunit of AMP-activated protein kinase, the cell's central energy sensor governing glucose and fatty acid metabolism. Activating or dysregulating variants disturb this energy-sensing function, causing excessive accumulation of glycogen within cardiomyocytes. Glycogen-laden myocytes produce ventricular hypertrophy that resembles hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, and glycogen deposition also disrupts the annulus fibrosus, allowing anomalous atrioventricular connections that generate ventricular pre-excitation. Progressive infiltration and degeneration of the conduction system cause worsening atrioventricular block over time, while the accessory conduction and atrial disease predispose to tachyarrhythmias. The disorder is thus a metabolic (glycogen storage) cardiomyopathy with a distinctive electrophysiological signature.
additionalDifferentials: Fabry disease and other storage cardiomyopathies
additionalInvestigations: 12-lead ECG for pre-excitation, short PR interval and conduction abnormalities
Echocardiography to assess the pattern and degree of hypertrophy
Cardiac MRI to characterise myocardium and distinguish from sarcomeric and infiltrative disease
Ambulatory ECG monitoring for tachyarrhythmia and progressive block
Genetic testing of PRKAG2 with cascade family screening
Assessment to exclude other storage disorders (for example Fabry and Danon disease)
redFlags: Rapidly conducted atrial fibrillation in the presence of an accessory pathway
Progression to high-grade atrioventricular block or symptomatic bradycardia
Severe or rapidly progressive hypertrophy with impaired function
reference.prognosis: The disorder tends to progress over years, with many patients ultimately needing pacing for conduction disease and management of tachyarrhythmias; heart failure can develop in advanced disease, and prognosis is improved by early rhythm surveillance and device therapy.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing it as sarcomeric hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and missing the glycogen storage basis
Overlooking pre-excitation as a clue to the underlying metabolic disorder
Underestimating the risk of rapidly conducted atrial fibrillation via an accessory pathway
Neglecting family screening for an autosomal dominant condition
